title: Transient egress-path collision during node drains causes DNS mis-resolution between tenants
creator: Aisha Kumar
description: Summary: A customer flagged intermittent cross-tenant DNS resolutions and unexplained 5xxs during Dedicated node drain events. Investigation shows a narrow window during autoscaler/rolling-drain where egress dataplane path reallocation and resolver UDP socket reuse combined to deliver DNS responses to the wrong tenant flow, causing tenant A to receive tenant B's DNS answers.
reproduction_steps: 1) Provision two tenants on the same Dedicated pool with VPC peering enabled between peer networks.
2) Configure both tenants to use the platform resolver (UDP) and ensure short TTL test records (5s) on an external authoritative server.
3) Start sustained parallel DNS-heavy workloads from both tenants to create high ephemeral port churn.
4) Trigger a controlled rolling drain of a subset of GPU nodes to force egress dataplane reassignment and NAT mapping churn.
5) Observe DNS queries/responses: intermittent mismatches occur within a <500ms window after the dataplane path switch.
6) Capture pcap on the host dataplane and compare source ports, connection tuples, and resolver mappings to reproduce the mis-association.
Result: Some DNS responses were accepted by the wrong tenant's socket due to overlapping ephemeral port reuse and short-lived route rewrite during the drain/peering update path.

Logs and artifacts: pcap captures in s3://redwood-debug/ENG-72801/pcaps/, dashboard link https://grafana.redwood.internal/d/ENG-72801-dns-bleed, reproduction script https://github.com/redwood-inference/incidents/tree/ENG-72801/repro
root_cause: During node drain and dataplane reprogramming we observed two contributing factors: (A) ephemeral UDP source port reuse on the host NAT layer was faster than our tenant socket lifecycle expectation, and (B) the dataplane's route rewrite path briefly forwarded resolver replies to the old namespace before conntrack entries were reconciled. The combination allowed a DNS response packet to match an unrelated socket tuple after port reuse, resulting in incorrect resolution being delivered across tenant flows.
mitigation: 1) Immediate customer-side mitigation provided: increase DNS TTLs and reduce concurrent ephemeral port churn where possible.
2) Short-term platform mitigation rolled to canary: add a 1s hold-off timer in dataplane reprogramming path that delays route swap until conntrack cleanup is observed.
3) Emergency config: enable per-tenant resolver sockets bound to non-ephemeral port ranges for high-risk tenants (config toggle).
4) Monitoring: added dashboard panels for resolver RTT, ephemeral port churn rate, conntrack deletion lag, and per-tenant DNS mismatch alerts.
5) Customer communication: emailed affected customers with incident summary and mitigation steps; support playbook updated.
roll_out_plan: 1) Merge fix PR and run unit + integration tests in CI.
2) Deploy to staging dedicated cluster and run repro suite (repro script linked above).
3) Canary deploy to 10% of Dedicated pools with active DNS-heavy tenants for 48h while monitoring mismatch alerting.
4) If stable, ramp to 100% over 12h and remove emergency hold-off after 72h if metrics normalise.
5) Post-deploy: run synthetic cross-tenant DNS flood tests weekly for two cycles to validate regression.
postmortem_actions: 1) Implement permanent fix to ensure resolver replies are elastically isolated by attaching unique flow tags to UDP sockets to avoid port-based ambiguity.
2) Re-evaluate ephemeral port allocation strategy and extend port quarantine window during dataplane reconfiguration.
3) Add an e2e test in CI that simulates node drains under heavy DNS churn to prevent regressions.
4) Update runbook: include immediate steps for on-call to identify and mitigate this class of cross-tenant response issues.
5) Schedule design review for long-term dataplane conntrack reconciliation improvements (eng/arch deep dive).
